content: Halite is the mineral form of sodium chloride (NaCl), commonly referred to as rock salt. It crystallizes in an isometric system, forming cubic crystals. The mineral is typically colorless to yellow but can also appear in shades of light blue, dark blue, and pink. Halite is often found in association with other evaporite minerals, including sulfates, halides, and borates. Halite is commonly found in extensive beds of sedimentary evaporite minerals, which form as a result of the evaporation of enclosed bodies of water such as lakes, playas, and seas. These salt beds can reach thicknesses of up to 405 meters and cover large geographic areas. In North America, significant underground halite deposits are located in the Appalachian Basin of western New York, parts of Ontario, and much of the Michigan Basin. Additional deposits are found in Ohio, Kansas, New Mexico, Nova Scotia, and Saskatchewan. Salt domes, which are vertical diapirs or pipe-like masses of salt, form when underlying salt beds are mobilized and pushed upward due to the weight of overlying rock. These domes often contain other minerals such as anhydrite, gypsum, and native sulfur, in addition to halite and sylvite. Salt domes are prevalent along the Gulf coasts of Texas and Louisiana and are frequently associated with petroleum deposits. Similar structures are also found in Germany, Spain, the Netherlands, Romania, and Iran. In arid regions of Iran, salt glaciers have formed where salt has broken through the surface at high elevations and flows downhill. In such cases, halite exhibits rheological behavior, meaning it flows under stress over geological timescales. Unusual purple, fibrous vein-filling halite has been discovered in France and a few other locations. Halite crystals known as hopper crystals appear as skeletal forms of typical cubes, with edges intact and stepped depressions on each crystal face. These form in rapidly crystallizing environments where the edges of the cubes grow faster than their centers. Halite crystals can form quickly in rapidly evaporating lakes, creating modern artifacts coated or encrusted with halite. Rare halite formations, such as halite flowers, are curling fibers of halite found in arid caves, such as those in Australia's Nullarbor Plain. Halite stalactites and encrustations have also been reported in the Quincy native copper mine in Hancock, Michigan. Halite has practical applications, particularly in ice management. When salt is applied to ice, it lowers the freezing point of water, causing the ice to melt. This property is widely utilized by homeowners in cold climates, who spread rock salt on walkways and driveways after snowstorms to weaken the ice, making it easier to remove. Municipalities often use a mixture of sand and salt on roads during and after snowstorms to improve traction. Additionally, rock salt is used in the process of making ice cream. While it is not added to the ice cream mixture itself, it is used to melt the ice surrounding the container holding the ice cream. This melting process lowers the temperature of the ice bath, accelerating the freezing of the ice cream.
